_comment: Estonian (et). Same Finnic-family register choice as fi.json: the done/past slot uses the impersonal (umbisikuline) past participle (Fail kustutatud), the progress/gerund slot uses the impersonal present (Kustutatakse...) — the genuine Estonian software convention for status/result text. No articles, no grammatical gender (both correctly omitted). DESIGN DECISION — the noun 'other' slot carries the PARTITIVE SINGULAR, not the nominative plural: Estonian numerals govern the partitive singular (3 viga, never *3 vead), and in an article-less locale the count path is the only consumer of 'other' (no plural articles and no suffixed definites exist to reuse the slot), so 'other' is free to carry the numeral-governed form; 'one' stays nominative singular, which is what the numeral 1 governs (1 fail). For viga and haru the partitive singular is homophonous with the nominative — that is the grammar, not an omission. The verb table is keyed by the DA-infinitive (kustutada, not the ma-infinitive kustutama) deliberately: Estonian's natural 'failed to' construction (ei õnnestunud + verb) grammatically requires the da-infinitive, and ActionFailed() composes the bare bridge/base value directly with no further conjugation — so the da-infinitive is the one form that keeps every composed slot grammatical at once. Lower-confidence entries, flagged here rather than silently omitted: 'commit' bridges to salvestada (general 'save', mirroring fi.json's tallentaa — Estonian git vocabulary is unsettled and loanword-heavy in practice); 'push' bridges to lükata (the correct, common literal 'push' verb — cf. real Lükka/Tõmba door signage — but its git-specific adoption is unconfirmed, and its impersonal forms lükatakse/lükatud are derived by regular pattern rather than a directly attested UI string); 'merge' bridges to ühendada, which as commonly reads 'connect/join' as a git-specific merge. Residual case limitation, now confined to fail.*: the object after 'Ei õnnestunud + infinitive' renders in the nominative ('one' form) where Estonian properly wants the partitive — the subject slot is shared with positions that need the nominative, so it cannot carry case; the count path, where the partitive is obligatory, is correct. 'item' -> ese (object/item) is a defensible but not uniquely-correct rendering of a genuinely abstract English word.
